title: The in-between again
hookLine: families who count the days after a death in sevens, here and in Genesis
tomorrow: how would you want to be cared for at the end?

cards: After a death, the casseroles come for a week or two, and then they stop. The texts stop. Everyone goes back to normal, and the person grieving is suddenly alone with it.
A month later, the grief can be just getting started. Some families refuse to let it stop that fast. They count.
A ceremony on the seventh day, then the fourteenth, all the way to the forty-ninth. So why forty-nine days? One question today, and an answer from Tibet.

teach.b: Tibetan Buddhism teaches the bardo, the in-between: a passage between one life and the next. The Tibetan text read near the dead describes it unfolding over as many as forty-nine days, in weeks of seven.
Visions arise, peaceful and fierce, and over and over the text urges the one who has died to recognize them as the mind's own light and not be afraid. So the living help.

They read the text aloud, make offerings, and dedicate the good of it to the one who died. Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese Buddhist families keep rites on the seventh days too, ending on the forty-ninth.
Not every school teaches an in-between; Theravada teachers generally hold that rebirth follows at once. Here's something shared.

teach.h: SEVEN DAYS OF MOURNING IN GENESIS.
teach.b: In the book of Genesis, when Jacob dies, his son Joseph and the whole household stop at a threshing floor across the Jordan, and the text says "he made a mourning for his father seven days."
Jewish families still keep a week of mourning at home, called shiva. Two traditions, both giving grief a counted shape, so it isn't rushed. And one honest difference.

teach.h: FOR THE MOURNERS, OR FOR THE DEAD TOO.
teach.b: In Genesis the seven days belong to the mourners.
In the bardo teaching, the forty-nine days are also the journey of the one who died, and the family's counting is a way of walking beside them.

how: Tibetan families ask lamas to read the Bardo Thodol and make offerings during the forty-nine days; Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese Buddhist families hold memorial rites every seventh day, ending with a larger ceremony on the forty-ninth.

games.q: three weeks after a funeral, your friend says everyone acts like she should be over it. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: three weeks is plenty; she should try to move on now.
grief deserves a counted, unhurried time; you can keep checking in.
she should count exactly forty-nine days and then stop grieving.
games.why: both traditions give grief a counted shape so it isn't rushed. the count is a kindness, not a deadline.

practice: Find a photo of someone who has died, or an object that was theirs, or simply hold their face in mind. If no one comes to mind, hold someone who is grieving now. Look at it for the whole sit, without hurrying.
Before the bell, decide on one small way you'll remember them over the next seven weeks.

wordCard.voice: The in-between again: the bardo, the passage after death in Tibetan teaching, counted out in weeks of seven, with the living walking beside.

orig.note: Sanskrit antarabhava: the in-between existence; bardo is the Tibetan word.

carryVoice: For the road: forty-nine days, grief with a count so nobody has to hurry it. Twenty-six of thirty, counted.
